B Per the USPSTF, there is insufficient data to make a recommendation for or against screening in men. Other national organizations differ primarily in their recommendations for screening in men.

background.definition: Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder characterized by compromised bone strength predisposing a person to increased fracture risk.

list.listitem: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the incidence rate for hip fracture among Medicare beneficiaries is 73.9/10,000.
The hip fracture rate in men is about one-third the hip fracture rate in women of the same age.

Based on data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2005 to 2010, the prevalence of osteoporosis at either the femoral neck or lumbar spine was 16.2% of adults over age 65 years, ranging from 24.8% in women and 5.6% in men. Almost half (48.3%) of older adults have low bone mass at these sites.
Among adults over age 50 years, osteoporosis affects 10.3% of the US population which translates into an estimated 10.2 million adults according to data from the CDC.
Half of all postmenopausal women will have an osteoporosis-related fracture in their lifetime; 15% of postmenopausal women will have a hip fracture in their lifetime.
Five percent of 50-year-old women and 25% of 80-year-old women have had at least one vertebral fracture.
About 1 in 5 older men are at risk of an osteoporosis-related fracture.

Among individuals with COPD, authors of a meta-analysis of 58 studies found a pooled global prevalence of osteoporosis of 38% (95% CI 34%-43%). Other significant risk factors for osteoporosis in these patients were BMI <18.5 kg/m2 (OR 4.26) and the presence of sarcopenia (OR 3.65).
Direct cost of the treatment of osteoporotic fractures is $10 billion to $15 billion per year in the United States.
Up to 20% of women die within 1 year of a hip fracture.
Over 50% of women will be unable to return to independent living after a hip fracture.
Vertebral fractures can cause severe pain and lead to 150,000 hospital admissions per year in the United States.
Primary osteoporosis is caused by aging in men and women and the onset of menopause in women.

In addition, osteoporosis is also associated with genetic factors; in a Chinese study, osteoporosis was associated with the insulin-like growth factor-1 single nucleotide polymorphism rs35767. Variations in the COL1A1 gene are also associated with osteoporosis risk.
Secondary osteoporosis is caused by medical conditions or medication exposures that lead to increased bone loss (see ).
In men, 30% to 60% of osteoporotic fractures are associated with secondary causes.
Long-term use of proton pump inhibitors also increases the risk of fracture.
Statin therapy does not increase the risk of fracture.
Women using depot medroxyprogesterone acetate are at higher risk of bone loss, especially if they smoke and have low calcium intake.
See Risk Factors table below.

Bone strength reflects both bone density and quality. Approximately 70% of bone strength can be measured with bone mineral density (BMD) testing. Diminished bone strength leads to increased risk of fracture.
Bone mass peaks near age 30 years and then decreases over a lifetime in both men and women.
Menopause accelerates bone remodeling, leading to decreased bone strength.
A high rate of bone loss is associated with certain medical conditions (eg, hyperthyroidism) and medications (eg, glucocorticoids).
An increase in fall risk in the elderly is associated with an increased risk of hip and vertebral fractures.

list.listitem: The USPSTF (2025) recommends screening for osteoporosis in women 65 years of age and older and postmenopausal women younger than age 65 years at increased risk of osteoporosis, as determined by a formal clinical risk assesment tool (eg, those with a baseline risk similar to a 65-year-old which is 9.3% risk over 10 years on the FRAX fracture risk assessment tool) (2018).B

The USPSTF (2018) found insufficient evidence to recommend daily supplementation with doses >400 IU of vitamin D and >1000 mg of calcium for the primary prevention of fractures in community-dwelling, postmenopausal women and recommend against use of daily supplementation of lower amounts of vitamin D and calcium for these women.A These recommendations do not apply to persons with a history of osteoporotic fractures, increased risk for falls, or a diagnosis of osteoporosis or vitamin D deficiency.

Screening decisions should be individualized for all other groups; screening for men over age 75 years with risk factors is recommended by National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE 2017, update), American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE) and the National Osteoporosis Foundation (NOF). C
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is the accepted gold standard for measuring bone density.C

Calcium and vitamin D as primary prevention for community-dwelling adults without elevated fracture risk is not likely beneficial, but supplementation may be useful in elderly patients; data are conflicting. B

The USPSTF recommends screening for osteoporosis in women 65 years of age and older and for postmenopausal women younger than 65 years at increased risk of osteoporosis, as determined by a formal clinical risk assessment tool (2018). The UPSTF found insufficient evidence to recoment screening for osteoporosis in men.

The updated evidence report supported this recommendation by noting a possibility of screening reducing hip fracture rates and treatment of women with osteoporosis reducing both vertebral and nonvertebral fractures, depending on the medication selected. 29946734 Evidence supporting screening in men was supported by only a single trial showing reduced risk of radiographic vertebral fractures with zoledronic acid but no studies demonstrating reductions in clinical or hip fractures.

NICE concurs with recommendations for women but also recommends screening in men aged 75 years and older with risk factors (eg, prior fragility fracture, falls). The AACE, in response to the USPSTF draft statement, suggest screening be considered for men ages 70 or older in keeping with recommendations from the NOF guidelines, and for men at higher risk including those suffering a low trauma fracture, those with known hypogonadism or receiving anti-androgenic therapy, those receiving glucocorticoids, and those with a family history of hip fracture.

The most recently published UK screening trial of over 12,000 women aged 70 to 85 years reported no overall reduction in the rate of clinical fractures (15%), mortality or quality of life over 5 years. 200525 Women randomized to FRAX with offer of DEXA based on score and subsequent rating as high or low fracture risk reported to the patient and her physician were more likely than control women to be taking a osteoporotic medication (15% vs. 4% in year 1 and 15% vs. 10% in year 5) and had fewer hip fractures (2.6% vs. 3.5%; NNT 117; 95% CI 69-396).

Authors of the NICE guideline, Osteoporosis Fragility Fracture urge caution in interpreting the estimated absolute risk of fracture in people aged over 80 years, as predicted 10-year fracture risk may underestimate the short-term fracture risk. Likewise, fracture risk may be underestimated in individuals with a history of multiple fractures, vertebral fractures, high alcohol intake, and in those taking high-dose systemic corticosteroids or drugs that can impair bone metabolism (eg, anticonvulsants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, proton pump inhibitors and antiretroviral drugs).
Clinical decision rules such as the OST,SCORE, ORAI,NOF, and the Dutch instrument can help clinicians decide which patients should have bone density measured (see ).
Screening should be done using DEXA of the hip or lumbar spine or quantitative ultrasonography of the calcaneus. However, cutoffs for diagnosis and treatment have not been defined for ultrasound.
Calcaneal ultrasound, quantitative CT of the spine, and DEXA of the hip and spine can all help predict fracture risk, but DEXA is recommended by USPSTF as the preferred test.

In patients who have been screened and are not undergoing treatment for osteoporosis, the optimal interval for repeat screening has been studied. Repeat screening is unlikely to be beneficial more often than every 2 years except in those with severe osteopenia (T-score −2 to −2.49). Longer intervals should be considered in women at lower risk of fracture. Women with normal bone density (T-score >−1.0) or mild osteopenia (T-score −1.0 to −1.49) are unlikely to benefit from repeat screening within 15 years. Women with moderate osteopenia (T-score −1.5 to −1.99) can be screened again in 5 years.
Multiple BMD measurements over time are of minimal utility. Change in BMD does not more accurately predict fracture risk than a single measurement.

Rechecking BMD after 3 years did not add additional prognostic information in a 12-year follow-up study of 7419 women enrolled in the Women's Health Initiative study. In this study, 1.9% of women experienced a hip fracture and 9.9% had a major osteoporotic fracture. A change in BMD over 3 years or a combination of change in BMD with baseline BMD did not predict subsequent hip or major fracture to a greater degree than the initial BMD measure alone.
Bone mineral density (BMD) testing is recommended when starting patients on long-term glucocorticoid therapy. A clinical rule can help determine their risk of fracture. C
The Male Osteoporosis Risk Estimation Score (MORES) may be a useful screening test for hip-fracture risk in men. It is a simple point score that uses age, presence of COPD, and weight.

In one study comparing risk assessment tools in men, the OST had slightly better discrimination for identifying T-score-defined osteoporosis than the FRAX (area under the curve 0.68 vs. 0.62, respectively).
All patients, especially those with osteoporosis, should be counseled to quit smoking.

Weight-bearing exercise including aerobics, resistance training, and walking increases BMD at the hip or spine in postmenopausal women. Most effective for increased femoral neck BMD was nonweight bearing high force exercise (eg, progressive resistance strength training for the lower limbs). Most effective for increased BMD of the spine was combination exercise programs.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 59 studies, including 12 observational studies and 47 trials, concluded that physical activity interventions probably improve lumbar spine BMD (standardized effect size 0.17, 95% CI 0.04-0.30, moderate-certainty evidence) and may improve hip (femoral neck) BMD. Higher doses of physical activity (60+ minutes, 2-3 times/weekly for 7 or more months) and programs involving multiple exercise types or resistance exercise appear to be most effective.

AACE also recommends limiting alcohol to no more than two servings per day and possibly limiting caffeine intake. Tea consumption, however, appears protective (OR highest to lowest consumption category 0.62 (95% CI 0.46-0.83).
High intake of fish (>2 servings per week) is associated with maintenance of femoral neck BMD in men and women.

Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake and exercise in children and young adults contributes to a higher peak bone mass, although evidence does not support calcium supplementation as a public health intervention in children.

In a population study in Sweden, fracture risk was highest for women in the lowest quintile of dietary calcium intake especially if low in vitamin D; above that quintile, increasing dietary calcium was not associated with increasing protection against fracture or osteoporosis (nonlinear relationship).
Women and men at risk of fracture should consume 1000 to 1200 mg of calcium daily and 400 to 800IU of vitamin D.
A large meta-analysis showed use of calcium and Vitamin D in community dwelling elderly is not associated with improved incidence of fractures.

In a systematic review and evidence report for the USPSTF on the role of calcium and vitamin D as primary prevention for community-dwelling adults without known vitamin D deficiency, osteoporosis, or prior fracture, authors concluded that Vitamin D supplementation alone or with calcium was not associated with reduced fracture incidence, including hip fracture, and increases the risk of kidney stones.

Calcium and vitamin D intake appear to be important in the elderly to reduce the likelihood of first hip fracture. A recent meta-analysis of 10 studies of primarily elderly subjects found that calcium and vitamin reduced risk of total fractures (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) and hip fractures (RR: 0.61, 95% CI 0.4-0.92), but study heterogeneity was high.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 49,282 participants, 5,449 fractures, 730 hip fractures found combined supplementation with vitamin D and calcium at these doses reduced risk of any fracture by 6% (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89-0.99) and hip fracture risk by 16% (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72-0.97).

Based on a meta-analysis of RCTs of combined calcium and vitamin D supplementation for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women also found improved BMD at all sites and significantly reduced incidence of hip fracture (RR 0.864, 95% CI 0.763-0.979).

A single study showed that a single large dose of vitamin D of 100,000 IU given orally every 4 months for 5 years reduced fractures in 20 elderly British women.A systematic review supported these findings, particularly in nursing home patients. Interestingly, another study found that women randomized to 700 to 1000 IU of vitamin D per day were also less likely to fall (NNT = 11).

However, vitamin D alone in currently recommended doses is unlikely to prevent new fracture or hip fracture, based on high quality evidence. In addition, treating low vitamin D levels in postmenopausal women with the usual dose of vitamin D (800 IU daily) does not increase vitamin D levels even after a year of therapy and has little effect on calcium absorption or bone mineral density.

Treating postmenopausal women with high dose vitamin D (twice monthly 50,000 IU vitamin D3) to achieve and maintain vitamin D levels >30 ng/mL marginally improved calcium absorption but did not improve BMD, muscle function, muscle mass, or falls at 1 year. In addition, in a 3-year RCT of 311 community-dwelling healthy men and women without osteoporosis, aged 55 to 70 years, with normal baseline levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the 2 groups randomized to daily high-dose (4,000 IU or 10,000 IU) had statistically significant lower radial BMD and lower tibial BMD in the 10,000 IU per day group than the group taking 400 IU daily, and there were no significant differences in bone strength between groups at either the radius or tibia.
Calcium with or without vitamin D increases the risk of myocardial infarction (RR 1.24; 1.07-1.45) and may increase the risk of stroke.

Patients on corticosteroids are at increased risk for fractures. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommends calcium, Vitamin D, and lifestyle changes in all patients on chronic glucocorticoids.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 prospective cohort studies on dietary antioxidant vitamin intake including 384,464 individuals found increased vitamin E intake to be associated with reduced fracture risk (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.46-0.95) which not observed for increased vitamin A or C intake. Multivitamin intake was associated with reduced hip fragility fracture risk based on a meta-analysis of eight studies.

Hormone therapy (HT) as primary prevention reduces fracture risk by -53 cases per 10,000 person-years for estrogen alone and -44 per 10,000 person-years for combination HT. Risks include 30 more cases of gallbladder disease 11 more cases of stroke, 11 more cases of venous thromboembolism and 1261 more cases of urinary incontinence for estrogen alone. For combination HT, there are 9 more cases of invasive breast cancer, 22 more cases of probable dementia, 21 more cases of gallbladder disease, 9 more cases of stroke, 21 more cases of venous thromboembolism, and 876 more cases of urinary incontinence.

HT can be offered to women at significant fracture risk for whom non-estrogen therapies are unsuitable.The risk of fracture is reduced after 5.6 years' use of combination HT (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.71-0.86). In women without a uterus using estrogen-only HT, fracture risk is similarly reduced (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65-0.80). A 2016 Cochrane review found similar results. The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends against use of estrogens or raloxifene for osteoporosis.

Authors of a Cochrane review found no benefit of risedronate 5 mg/day on wrist fractures, based on low-certainty evidence, and no evidence regarding clinical vertebral or hip fractures from 4 trials including 989 postmenopausal women at lower risk of fractures.

For patients on chronic glucocorticoids, use of bisphosphonates reduces the risk of vertebral fractures (77/1000 incident fractures for placebo vs. 44/1000 for intervention group), with a NNT of 31. There is no benefit for nonvertebral fractures.

Bisphosphonate therapy should be considered in all patients starting glucocorticoid therapy with a duration planned for over 3 months. The ACR recommends estimating FRAX score and assessing bone density within 6 months of starting glucocorticoids and reassessing fracture risk anually. ACR recommends bisphosphonates as first-line therapy for glucocorticoid-associated osteoporosis.

According to one expert panel, patients on chronic glucocorticoid therapy should be treated with a bisphosphonate if the T-score on DEXA is less than −1.0.Among individuals with cystic fibrosis who are at higher risk of OP, bisphosphonates consistently increased lumbar spine and hip BMD but did not reduce rates of fractures or death.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 19 unique studies with 4328 patients found that teriparatide (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.03-0.47), denosumab (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.09-0.49), and risedronate (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.19-0.58) reduced risk of glucocorticoid-associated vertebral fractures; the former 2 were the most effective. Benefit was also seen for oral alendronate (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.12-0.93) in patients receiving glucocorticoids with at least 7.5 mg/day and intravenous ibandronate (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.06-0.99) for primary prevention of fractures.

The Endocrine Society 2019 guideline recommends use of calcium and vitamin D as an adjunct to osteoporosis therapies for women with low bone mineral density and at high risk of fractures with osteoporosis, and for women with osteoporosis who are unable to tolerate osteoporosis therapies to prevent hip fractures.
Women with osteoporosis who have 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of <20 ng/mL should take 1000 IU of vitamin D daily.
The operational definition of osteoporosis is a BMD value of 2.5 SD or more below the mean for a young female adult assessed by DEXA at the spine or femoral neck.C

Secondary, potentially reversible, causes of osteoporosis should be identified by history, physical, or laboratory examination (). Secondary causes should be considered when a patient's Z-score is less than −2.0. C

The Endocrine Society (2019) guidelines recommend screening for vitamin D deficiency; 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels in women with osteoporosis should be at least 20 ng/mL which can be achieved by ingesting 1000 IU of vitamin D daily. B
T-score is the difference, described in number of SDs, in BMD compared with young adults of the same gender.
Z-score is the difference, described by number of SDs, in BMD compared with adults of the same age and gender.
The World Health Organization defines osteoporosis as a T-score less than −2.5 SD or a history of fragility fracture and osteopenia as a T-score between −1 and −2.5 SD.
Osteoporosis should be suspected in older patients with kyphosis.
Many cases of osteoporosis and people at increased risk of fracture will only be detected by measurement of BMD.
A focused history can identify patients at increased risk of fracture.
DEXA measurement of BMD is the accepted gold standard in the diagnosis of osteoporosis.
Although other imaging modalities such as calcaneal ultrasound and quantitative CT can aid in estimating fracture risk, treatment decisions should be based on DEXA.

DEXA was also useful in identifying prevalent vertebral fractures in asymptomatic postmenopausal women based on a meta-analysis of 28 studies. Pooled prevalence of fractures was 28% (95% CI 23%-32%), and up to 43% of women had osteopenia and up to 32% had normal bone density.

TBS is an image-based software technique to measure bone texture correlated with bone microarchitecture. TBS can be used as an adjunct to BMD measurement and FRAX. In a population-based registry study in Manitoba, Canada of 34,316 women with baseline spine and hip DEXA, FRAX-based fracture probability measurements, lumbar spine TBS, and minimum 5 years of observation, 3503 had an incident non-traumatic major osteoporotic fracture and 945 had an incident hip fracture. The proportions of women reclassified with the TBS adjustment to FRAX were less than 5% with >90% of the reclassification occurring close to the intervention threshold. This resulted in a small but significant net reclassification improvement by using lumbar spine TBS to adjust FRAX probability.

However, in a study of 358 Iranian women undergoing BMD and TBS testing, 184 had osteopenia and 21 had vertebral fractures; the addition of TBS to BMD or FRAX did not improve predictive value for vertebral fracture or change treatment decisions.

Radius quantitative ultrasound (radial speed of sound [SOS]) may be useful in identifying fracture risk. In a meta-analysis of 13 studies with 16,681 individuals, for each standard deviation decrease in radial SOS, risk of overall fragility fracture increased by 21% and hip fracture increased by 55%.

Authors of a cost-effectiveness model, however, concluded that combined quantitative computed tomography (CT) and DEXA starting at age 55 years and followed by quantitative CT screening every 5 years was the most cost-effective screening tool for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women. They estimated that this strategy would result in 12.8% of postmenopausal women sustaining a hip fracture in their remaining life compared to 18.7% with no screening and 15.8% with DEXA screening alone.
A number of validated clinical decision rulescan help identify women at higher than average risk of fracture. ORAI is shown in .
A clinical prediction rule has also been developed and validated to predict the risk of fracture in corticosteroid users.

The FRAX score has been well validated in a range of populations and is recommended by many guidelines; use the country-specific version. It can be found at this site, select Calculation Tool and then your population (ie, North America).

Screen women for osteoporosis if they are 65 years or older; screen younger postmenopausal women at increased risk of fracture (those with a baseline risk similar to a 65-year-old). DEXA scan is the preferred test.
Patient preferences should be incorporated into treatment planning.

Incorporate lifestyle interventions (smoking cessation, exercise), fall prevention, and nutritional interventions to ensure adequate vitamin D and calcium intake, in addition to pharmacotherapy to prevent fractures.

A patient's 10-year absolute fracture risk, including both clinical and BMD factors, should be considered prior to the initiation of medical therapy (see or the online FRAX tool to estimate fracture risk). This approach has more clinical utility than treatment based solely on BMD thresholds. Addition of TBS to adjust FRAX probability may be helpful for those close to the treatment threshold. Risk of fracture can be estimated based on age and T-score () and/or on risk-factor assessment ().

The European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis and the Committees of Scientific Advisors and National Societies of the International Osteoporosis Foundation recommend consideration of vertebral fracture assessment if there is a history of ≥4cm height loss, kyphosis, recent or current long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy, or a BMD T-score ≤ -2.5.
Postmenopausal women who are at high risk of fractures, especially those who have experienced a recent fracture, should be considered for pharmacotherapy.
Benefits of treatment are summarized in . Many pharmacologic therapies are available for reducing fracture rates in postmenopausal women at risk with acceptable risk-benefit and safety profiles.
Treat and identify secondary causes, and recommend exercise and smoking cessation. C

Vitamin D at about 800 IU/day Aand calcium at 1500 mg/day are recommended for women with osteoporosis at high risk of fractures as an adjunct to pharmacotherapy or alone in women unable to tolerate other therapies. A
Consider hip protectors for elderly nursing home patients. B
Medical therapy is indicated in women with osteoporosis. Alendronate has the strongest supporting evidence and prevents hip, vertebral, and non-vertebral fractures. A
For patients at very high risk of fracture (for example, recent fracture with a T score <-2.5) anabolic agents are recommended first line. B

Women with osteoporosis should be treated with medical therapy (see ). Some expert guidelines also recommend treating women with a T-score of less than −1.5 if they are at increased risk of fracture. One guideline recommends treatment with a 10-year hip fracture risk of 3% or a 10-year major osteoporosis-related fracture risk of 20%.

The Endocrine Society (2019), AACE and the American College of Physicians recommend alenronate, zoledronic acid, risedronate and denosumab as first-line therapy.In addition, vitamin D at 400 to 800 IU and calcium at 1000 to 1200 mg daily are recommended. Women with osteoporosis who have 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels of <20 ng/mL should take 1000 IU of vitamin D daily.

The evidence report for the USPSTF concluded that, for women, bisphosphonates, parathyroid hormone, raloxifene, and denosumab were associated with a lower risk of vertebral fractures based on 9 trials with 23 to 690 women (RRs 0.32-0.64) and that bisphosphonates and denosumab reduced risk of nonvertebral fracture, although only the latter appeared to reduce risk of hip fracture based on a single trial.

The 2024 guideline from the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research (ASBMR) and Bone Health & Osteoporosis Foundation (BHOF, formerly National Osteoporosis Foundation) identifies a category of patient at very high risk of fracture, including patients with a T score < -2.5 and a recent fracture. Anabolic agents were found to have better bone mineral density changes and fracture reduction compared with antiresorptive agents.
The ASBMR/BHOF guideline also recommends treating to BMD targets.

Alendronate has the strongest supporting evidence. Based on a Cochrane review of 11 studies, alendronate prevents hip (ARR 1%), vertebral (ARR 6%), and non-vertebral fractures (ARR 2%). For those unable to tolerate alendronate, risedronate, etidronate or strontium ranelate are recommended as possible alternative treatments to prevent fractures by NICE (Osteoporosis—primary prevention). Oral bisphosphonates should be taken in the morning, 30 minutes before food or drink with a full glass of water. Patients should stay in an upright position for 30 minutes after taking the medication. If taken correctly, there is little or no increased risk of GI tract problems with oral bisphosphonates.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs with 14,354 postmenopausal women at higher risk of fractures found that risedronate 5 mg/day probably prevents non‐vertebral fractures (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.90; absolute risk reduction [ARR] 2% fewer, 95% CI 1% fewer to 3% fewer) and may reduce hip fractures (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.94; ARR 1% fewer, 95% CI 0.2% fewer to 1% fewer).

For patients with osteoporosis who have experienced an osteoporosis-related fracture, subsequent treatment with a bisphosphonate resulted in a mortality benefit among patients hospitalized with a major fracture after 3 years of follow up (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.52 - 0.67), based on a national database including 101,115 patients with a diagnosis of osteoporosis who were hospitalized for a major fracture in Taiwan. However, authors of a 2020 meta-analysis including 38 RCTs with over 100,000 patients followed for at least 3 years did not find a mortality benefit from bisphosphonate treatment. The imbalance of risk factors in the former study as well as health user bias may partly explain the differences between these two studies

Among 2000 older women with osteopenia, those randomized to zoledronate 5 mg every 18 months vs. saline infusion had a reduced risk of symptomatic fractures, primarily nonvertebral fragility fractures at 31.2 and 46.9 per 1000 person-years, respectively; NNT was 64.

Minodronate, a third-generation bisphosphonate developed and approved for clinical use in osteoporosis therapy in Japan, had better clinical efficacy with respect to reduced vertebral fractures in patients with osteoporosis than other drugs (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.36–0.74) based on a meta-analysis of 13 studies with 3740 participants.

Adverse effects: Osteonecrosis of the jaw is rarely associated with bisphosphonate therapy, especially high-dose IV therapy. The estimated incidence with oral bisphosphonate therapy is 0.7 per 100,000 patient-years. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 studies of medication-related jaw osteonecrosis found a pooled weighted prevalence for bisphosphonates of 5% (95% CI 0%-9%), but higher risk with sequential therapy (10%; 95% CI 3%-22% for sequential ibandronate-zoledronate therapy 13%; 95% CI 3%-22% for sequential bisphosphonate-denosumab therapy and 19%; 95% CI 10%-27% for sequential pamidronate-zoledronate therapy).

Bisphosphonates are also associated with atypical femoral shaft fractures (0.13% in the subsequent year for women with at least 5 years of treatment), although the risk appears small (5/10,000 patient years). The UPSTF found adequate evidence that the harms of bisphosphonates are small.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. The recommended dose is 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months. The effects of denosumab on bone remodeling reverse after 6 months if the drug is not taken on schedule.

In a 3-year randomized-controlled trial (RCT), denosumab reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures in women with multiple and/or severe prevalent vertebral fractures (ARR 9.1%) and the risk of hip fractures in patients 75 years or older (ARR 1.4%).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies with 3540 patients with osteoporosis comparing denosumab with 1 of the bisphosphonates did not find differences in fracture risk (4% vs. 3.1%) or in osteoporotic fracture at 12 months based on three studies with 1999 patients (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.39-2.15). Osteonecrosis of the jaw among patients taking denosumab was reported at 4% (95% CI 3%-5%) in one meta-analysis. Drug cost is higher with denosumab compared to bisphosphonates.

Risks of treatment include a higher incidence of deep-seated infections such as endocarditis, cancer, and skin rash. Denosumab is very expensive and should be reserved for patients who are not tolerating bisphosphonates.
Denosumab also increases BMD in men with continued increases over 2 years; no fracture data were reported.

Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits sclerostin, increasing bone formation and decreasing bone resorption. The 2020 update to the Endocrine Society guidelines recommend romosozumab treatment at 210 mg monthly, subcutaneously, for up to 1 year for the reduction of vertebral, hip, and nonvertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at very high risk of fracture, such as those with severe osteoporosis (ie, low T-score < −2.5 and fractures) or multiple vertebral fractures. Women at high risk of cardiovascular disease (eg, myocardial infarction) and stroke, however, should not be considered for romosozumab until further studies on cardiovascular risk are completed.

In women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture, one year of monthly subcutaneous romosozumab prior to alendronate therapy compared to weekly alendronate alone, initiated at the same time, decreases risk of hip fracture at 2 years (NNT = 83). However, women who received romosozumab had an increased risk of cardiovascular events (16 vs. 6 cardiac ischemic events and 16 vs. 7 other cardiovascular events).

Teriparatide, a recombinant form of PTH, was compared with alendronate in patients with steroid-induced osteoporosis. While it appeared to provide greater protection at much greater cost, the 50% dropout rate in the study makes the findings highly suspect.

Authors of the NICE guideline Osteoporosis—Secondary Prevention recommend teriparatide under certain circumstances as a possible alternative treatment to prevent further fractures in women with a prior osteoporotic fracture, particularly for women whose BMD has fallen despite bisphosphonate treatment. AACE recommends its use for patients with very high fracture risk or patients in whom bisphosphonate therapy has failed. The Endocrine Society (2019 and 2020) recommend use of teriparatide or abaloparatide for up to 2 years in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at very high risk of fracture, such as those with severe or multiple vertebral fractures.

In a 3-arm RCT, both teriparatide or subcutaneous abaloparatide, a selective activator of the parathyroid hormone type 1 receptor, prevented new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures among postmenopausal women at risk of osteoporotic fracture vs. placebo at 18 months. There was less risk of hypercalcemia with abaloparatide vs. teriparatide (3.4% vs. 6.4%).

Adverse effects of abaloparatide and teriparatide were evaluated in women with osteoporosis participating in the phase 3 ACTIVE trial (2463 women), reported above, the extended ACTIVE trial (1139 women continued to 2 years), and a pharmacology study in 55 healthy adults. There were transient increases in HR and small decreases in BP among women among women on active treatment vs. placebo, but similar rates of serious cardiac adverse events of 0.9% to 1.0%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs, 5 at low risk of bias, with 1949 primarily post-menopausal women found lower incidences of clinical fracture (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.32-0.72), new vertebral fracture (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32-0.63), and non-vertebral fracture (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40-0.98) for those treated with teriparatide vs. risedronate with similar rates of adverse effects. Greater increases in BMD at all sites was also observed in the teriparatide group.

Authors of a meta-analysis of seven studies with 641 patients with osteoporosis found no differences in BMD or fracture risk at one year between combination PTH analogues with bisphosphonates vs. monotherapy. In another meta-analysis of 10 trials, 5 reporting fracture outcomes, combination therapy with PTH was superior to HT alone (RR, 0.31; 95% CI 0.12-0.81). Combination drug therapy is not recommended by AACE.
Alendronate for two years after treatment with 18 months of abaloparatide decreases fractures compared to placebo vs. alendronate.
The American College of Physicians gives a conditional recommendation for teriparatide treatment followed by bisphosphonate treatment in women at very high risk of fracture.

Raloxifene at both 60 mg/day and 120 mg/day was effective for reducing vertebral fractures (RR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5-0.8 and RR, 0.5; 95% CI 0.4-0.7, respectively) and increasing BMD at the femoral neck, but not reducing non-vertebral fractures in a 3-year RCT of 6828 women.

The SERM lasofoxifene is moderately effective at preventing fracture but increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE); the effect on all-cause mortality was unclear. A third-generation SERM bazedoxifene reduced risk of vertebral fracture [risk risks (RR 0.69; 95% CI 0.52-0.93) based on 4 RCT with no reported increase in VTE or other serious adverse events.

The Endocrine Society recommends either raloxifene or bazedoxifene for postmenopausal women at high fracture risk who also have a low risk of deep vein thrombosis and for whom bisphosphonates or denosumab are not appropriate, or with a high risk of breast cancer. NICE recommends against use of raloxifene for preventing fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who have not had a fracture, and ACP recommends against use of raloxifene for women with osteoporosis. AACE considers this a third-line agent.
Calcitonin nasal spray can be considered for women with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture who can’t tolerate other agents.
Calcitonin nasal spray use for 28 days was shown to significantly reduce spine pain in a small RCT including both men and women with nontraumatic osteoporotic vertebral crush fracture.

Intranasal calcitonin had no effect on chronic back pain intensity and functional capacity of osteoporotic women regardless of the presence of fractures, degenerative disorders or chronic back pain of non-specific etiology in one RCT.

When used for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and acute vertebral fracture, intramuscular (IM) elcatonin performed better than IM minordronic acid (a bisphosphonate) for reducing pain immediately after a vertebral fracture in a small open-label trial with 51 women; combined therapy similarly improved pain and also increased BMD.
Oral salmon calcitonin failed to prevent new vertebral or nonvertebral fractures in an RCT of 4665 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

Men: Zoledronic acid vs. placebo in one RCT reduced the likelihood of radiographically-detected fractures, but not clinical fractures in men. There was a small increase in myocardial infarction (absolute increase 1.2%) among men in the active treatment arm.
ACP recommends bisphosphonate treatment in men at high risk of fracture, but cites weak evidence.
Authors of a meta-analysis found no benefit with bisphosphonates for all clinical fractures in men.

Women with breast cancer: Zoledronic acid vs. delayed treatment prevented bone loss in postmenopausal women with breast cancer receiving letrozole at 5 years, but did not reduce the incidence of osteoporosis or fractures.

Patients with osteoporosis on glucocorticoid therapy: Authors of a meta-analysis of anti-osteoporosis agents in patients with osteoporosis taking glucocorticoid therapy concluded that teriparatide had the lowest incidence of vertebral fracture, ibandronate had the lowest incidence of non-vertebral fracture, raloxifene had the best effect in increasing lumbar spine BMD, and denosumab was best in increasing total hip BMD.

In one RCT, soy isoflavone supplementation with 200 mg daily did not increase BMD more than placebo after two years in menopausal women without significant osteoporosis who were also receiving calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Interestingly, there were significantly more women reporting hot flashes in the soy supplementation group (48.4% vs. 31.7%).
Authors of a meta-analysis of trials identified in nine international and Chinese databases found supporting evidence that acupuncture and moxibustion improve BMD.

Use of electroacupuncture as a sole treatment or an adjunct to other treatments may relieve OP-related pain compared with medications (mean difference -0.58, 95% CI -0.97 to -0.19 and mean difference -1.47, 95% CI -2.14 to -0.79, respectively) based on a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs involving 731 participants; high study heterogeneity was noted.
Regular weight-bearing exercise is recommended for patients with osteoporosis and patients at increased risk of fracture.

In an analysis of 9 prospective studies, investigators found a significant inverse relationship between increasing level of physical activity and risk of hip fracture, but not wrist fracture, in older women (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.91-0.96).

In a 3-arm RCT of 613 patients with an osteoporotic vertebral fracture, there was no difference in quality of life or muscle endurance at 1 year between those randomized to outpatient physiotherapy or exercise outpatient physiotherapy compared to a 1-hour single session of physiotherapy.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs investigating whole-body vibration training found pre-post improvements in lumbar spine BMD and significant differences in femoral neck BMD, the latter when analyzing studies that included postmenopausal women younger than 65 years. No fracture data were reported.

Hip protectors decrease hip fractures in elderly nursing home residents and should additionally be considered for patients with a history of fall, a history of hip fracture, or those with significant risk factors for falling.
Factors contributing to increased fall risk such as poor vision, use of sedative drugs, sensory deficits, and abnormal gait should be addressed.
AACE recommends use of proper body mechanics and consideration of referral for physical and occupational therapy to reduce fall risk.
Secondary causes of osteoporosis should be identified and treated. C
Lifestyle modifications including weight-bearing exercise and smoking cessation are important in the treatment of osteoporosis. C
Percutaneous vertebroplasty does not improve pain from vertebral osteoporotic fractures compared to a sham procedure.

ACP recommends treatment for up to 5 years only. There may be minimal benefit to continuing alendronate for more than 5 years. The optimal duration of therapy is unknown, and a decision to pursue longer term therapy (beyond 5 years) should include a shared decision with the patient and acknowledgement of benefits, harms, costs, and uncertainties.

Bisphosphonates are sequestered in bone and slowly re-released. In one study, after a baseline dose of intravenous zoledronate, BMD remained above baseline values for 2 to 3 years in the 1-mg group, 3 to 4 years in the 2.5-mg group and 5 or more years in the 5-mg group.

A cohort study showed an association between long term use of bisphosphonates (9-13 years) and increased risk of fracture in older women. In this subset of 5120 women, mean age 80 years, who were at a high risk of fractures, used oral bisphosphonates for at least 2 years, participated in the Women's Health Initiative study, and did not take other medications affecting bone metabolism, there were more fractures among those using bisphosphonates for 10 to 13 years than among women who used bisphosphonates for only 2 years (hazard ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.07-1.57). There was no significant association between intermediate-term use of bisphosphonates and fracture risk.

Based on observational data and expert opinion, the AACE recommends a “drug holiday” after 4 to 5 years of stability if osteoporosis is mild and after 10 years, for 1 to 2 years, if fracture risk is high. Drug therapy should be reinstituted if BMD shows a substantial decline, bone turnover markers increase, or a fracture occurs.

The Endocrine Society (2020) recommends assessment of fracture risk after 3 to 5 years, and women who remain at high risk of fractures should continue bisphosphonate therapy, whereas those who are at low-to-moderate risk of fractures should be considered for temporary discontinuation of bisphosphonate holiday for up to 3 to 5 years. They acknowledge that this recommendation is based on limited quality data and expert opinion. For those on a bisphosphonate holiday, reassess fracture risk at 2- to 4-year intervals and consider reinitiating osteoporosis therapy earlier than the 5-year suggested maximum if there is a significant decline in BMD, an intervening fracture, or other factors that alter clinical risk status. The potential benefits of long-term therapy must be balanced against risks of osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures.

For women who are taking denosumab, the Endocrine Society (2020) suggests reassessing fracture risk after 5 to 10 years and for women who remain at high risk of fractures to either continue denosumab or be treated with other osteoporosis therapies. For women who have completed a course of romosozumab, they recommend treatment with antiresorptive osteoporosis therapies to maintain bone mineral density gains and reduce fracture risk.

The Endocrine Society (2020) recommends that postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who have completed a course of teriparatide or abaloparatide, continue treatment with antiresorptive osteoporosis therapies to maintain BMD gains.

AACE recommends referral to an endocrinologist for patients with normal BMD who sustain a fracture without major trauma, cases with recurrent fracture or continued bone loss despite treatment, severe osteoporosis or patients with unusual features, or when there are complicating comorbidities such as renal failure or hyperparathyroidism.

Untreated, osteoporosis results in vertebral and hip fractures, with about half of all postmenopausal women having an osteoporosis-related fracture in their lifetime and 15% of women and 5% of men over age 80 years suffering a hip fracture. Treatment reduces these risks.

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 38 RCTs with over 100,000 patients did not find a mortality benefit with drug treatment of osteoporosis. This finding is in contrast to data from observational studies that link treatment with longer life; this may due to healthy user bias.

BMD monitoring has not been shown to increase adherence to medical therapy and is unreliable in monitoring response to treatment, especially after only 1 year. Therefore, the BMD of patients undergoing treatment for osteoporosis should be monitored no more often than every 2 years. C The Endocrine Society recommends monitoring BMD every 1 to 3 years to assess treatment response.
ACP suggests not monitoring bone density while on treatment.
Even for women who are not under treatment for osteoporosis, rechecking BMD after 3 years does not appear to add additional prognostic information.
Because most patients discontinue bisphosphonate therapy after 1 year, they should be regularly encouraged to continue therapy. C
More studies are needed to investigate the use of bone turnover markers. Currently their clinical use is not routinely recommended.

There have been few studies of bisphosphonates in children. While they appear to be safe, there are no data regarding fracture prevention in children at risk of secondary osteoporosis. Alendronate does not reliably improve BMD in children.
Calcium supplementation is not supported for healthy children, and data are lacking on the results of supplementation in children with metabolic disorders.
There is some evidence that physical activity promotes bone mineralization in preterm infants.

feature.caption: Medications That Prevent Fractures in Osteoporosis.
feature.feature_body:
Bisphosphonates
NNT References
Alendronate Strongest evidence base; prevents hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures (A); reduces vertebral fractures in men (B) 41 to prevent hip fracture in osteoporotic woman 75-79 over 5 years
24 to prevent nonvertebral fracture over 2 years in high-risk women
72 to prevent vertebral fracture over 2 years in high-risk women
Risedronate Prevents vertebral and nonvertebral fractures (A) 43 to prevent nonvertebral fracture over 2 years in high-risk women; 96 to prevent vertebral fracture over 2 years in high-risk women
Ibandronate Intermittent dosing prevents vertebral fractures in women with previous vertebral fractures (B); monthly dosing 21 to prevent additional vertebral fracture over 3 years in women with previous vertebral fracture
Zoledronic acid Annual intravenous dose prevents hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures (B); associated with an increased incidence of serious atrial fibrillation, NNH 125 (B) 91 to prevent hip fracture in older women over 3 years; 48 to prevent clinical vertebral fracture in older women in 3 years
Other
Raloxifene (SERM) Prevents vertebral fractures (A) 96 to prevent vertebral fracture over 2 years in high-risk women
Calcitonin Prevents vertebral fractures in women with previous fractures (B); nasal spray or subcutaneous injection; effective for pain in osteoporotic vertebral fractures (A) 12 to prevent additional vertebral fracture over 3 years in women with previous fracture. Improves BMD but no data on fracture for steroid induced osteoporosis
Estrogens Increased risk of breast cancer, stroke, coronary artery disease, and thromboembolic events; likely to prevent vertebral and nonvertebral fractures (A)
Teriparatide Prevents vertebral and nonvertebral fractures in very high-risk women with previous fractures (A); increases trabecular bone density; subcutaneous, expensive 11 to prevent vertebral fracture and 34 to prevent nonvertebral fracture over 21 months in high-risk women with a history of fracture
Tibolone Prevents vertebral and non-vertebral fractures (B) For every 1000 women treated for 1 year with tibolone, there will be approximately 9 fewer vertebral fractures, 7 fewer nonvertebral fractures, 2 fewer breast cancers, 1 fewer colon cancer, 2 more strokes, and 1 additional endometrial cancer
Denosumab Prevents clinical vertebral fractures and hip fractures (B) 56 to prevent clinical vertebral fracture. 200 to prevent hip fracture. Expensive. May lead to an increase in infection
Abbreviation: SERM, selective estrogen receptor modulator.
